title: US Inflation Cools to 3.5% in June as Gasoline Prices Retreat From War Highs
excerpt: The biggest monthly drop in consumer prices since April 2020, driven by falling energy costs, beat economist forecasts — but a renewed Iran conflict threatens to reverse the relief.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • US consumer prices fell 0.4% in June, marking the first decline since April 2020.
  • Annual inflation rate dropped to 3.5%, lower than the expected 3.8%.
  • Gasoline prices decreased by 9.7% due to a temporary US-Iran ceasefire.
  • Core inflation eased to 2.6% year-over-year, with shelter costs rising only 0.1%.
  • Markets reacted positively, but a 60% chance of a Fed rate hike remains.

  • US consumer prices fell 0.4% in June, the first monthly decline since April 2020, bringing the annual inflation rate to 3.5% — well below the 3.8% economists had expected.
  • Energy prices plunged 5.7% in a single month as a short-lived US-Iran ceasefire pushed gasoline prices down 9.7%, though they have since reversed course.
  • Core inflation, excluding food and energy, eased to 2.6% year-over-year, with shelter costs posting their smallest monthly gain since January 2021.
  • Markets rallied on the data, but traders still price in a 60% chance of a Fed rate hike by September amid renewed Middle East tensions.

US consumer prices posted their sharpest monthly decline in over six years in June, offering a reprieve from the inflation surge that has squeezed household budgets across the country. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Tuesday that the consumer price index fell 0.4% from May, while the annual inflation rate dropped to 3.5% from 4.2% — a far cooler reading than the 3.8% economists had forecast.

The pullback was driven overwhelmingly by falling energy costs. Gasoline prices tumbled 9.7% over the month as a fragile ceasefire between the United States and Iran, signed on June 17, briefly reopened the Strait of Hormuz and calmed oil markets. The national average at the pump dipped to $3.70 per gallon in June from a peak of $4.40 in mid-May, according to the Energy Information Administration.

A Short-Lived Respite

The relief proved fleeting. Last week, the ceasefire collapsed after commercial tankers came under fire in the Strait of Hormuz, triggering renewed military strikes. Gasoline prices have already reversed course, climbing to $3.86 per gallon, according to AAA data. President Trump announced Monday that the United States would reinstate a naval blockade of the strait, raising the prospect of further energy price spikes.

> **"Gasoline prices have already reversed course, climbing to $3.86 per gallon, according to AAA data."**

"It appears less likely that the Fed will raise rates over the next few meetings," said Jeffrey Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial. "However, we may still be at an inflection point, given the risk that the energy shock could spill over into other categories of consumer prices."

"Gasoline prices have already reversed course, climbing to $3.86 per gallon, according to AAA data."

Beneath the Headline

The better-than-expected reading extended beyond energy. Core CPI, which strips out volatile food and energy components, was flat month-over-month and rose 2.6% annually — down from 2.9% in May and below the 2.8% consensus. Motor vehicle insurance costs fell 2.0%, communication prices dropped 1.5%, and apparel declined 0.6%.

Shelter costs, the largest component of household spending, rose just 0.1% in June — the smallest monthly gain since January 2021. Hotel and motel room prices fell 2.3%, while owner's equivalent rent edged up 0.2%.

Food prices, however, remained sticky. Grocery costs climbed 0.2%, pushed by a 4.3% surge in egg prices and a 1.2% rise in dairy. Food prices were up 3.0% year-over-year. Coffee prices offered some relief, dropping 2.0%, while fruit and vegetable costs dipped 0.2%.

The Fed's Dilemma

Market Reactions to Inflation Data
›S&P 500 rose by 0.2%
›Nasdaq gained 1%
›Treasury yields fell
›Dollar weakened by 0.6%
›60% chance of Fed rate hike by September

The data landed as Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh appeared before Congress, telling lawmakers the central bank had "no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation." The Fed held its benchmark rate steady at 3.50%-3.75% in June but raised its inflation forecast for the fiscal year.

Markets responded positively: the S&P 500 rose 0.2% and the Nasdaq gained 1% at the open, while Treasury yields fell and the dollar weakened 0.6%. But traders continued to price in a 60% probability of a rate hike by September, reflecting uncertainty over whether the energy-driven improvement can hold.

"A positive resolution with Iran before the end of the summer is becoming increasingly important."

— Jeffrey Roach, Chief Economist, LPL Financial

What It Means for Indian Americans

The cooling inflation offers practical relief to households grappling with elevated costs. Lower gasoline prices directly reduce commuting and transportation expenses, while easing shelter costs — a major household budget item — could slow rent increases that have hit metro areas with large Indian American populations, including the San Francisco Bay Area, New Jersey, and Dallas-Fort Worth.

The picture is complicated by divergent trends in India, where retail inflation accelerated to 4.38% in June, breaching the Reserve Bank of India's 4% target for the first time in 17 months. The contrast underscores how Middle East tensions ripple differently through the two economies: while the US benefits when ceasefire-driven crude price dips translate to lower pump prices, India — the world's third-largest crude importer — faces persistent fuel cost pressures that are feeding into food and transport inflation.

Whether the June reprieve lasts depends largely on the trajectory of the Iran conflict. With oil prices rising to a four-week high and the US reimposing its naval blockade, the same geopolitical forces that drove inflation down in June may push it back up by August.
